chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 231 to 240, Kapilar's kurinji decade with the refrain தெய்யோ: by our reading the friend (once the girl) presses the hill lover in courtship, pointing to the girl's pallor and slipping bangles, the dream that shows him only asleep, the cold north wind, the ewe that waits and the tusker that embraces a stone, the scent of her hair on his chest, and at last proposing to go with him to his town now the mother knows.

231.reading: The friend asks the lord of the high mountain how he can bring himself to a parting that wears away the spotted gold of his girl's skin and spreads pallor over it.
231.nuance: யாங்கு வல்லுநையோ asks how he is able: the strength he shows in staying away is set against the strength draining from her, so the question is a reproach that pushes him toward marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero is addressed as lord of the high mountain

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; she speaks of the girl in the third person to the hill lord, urging him to end the parting

232.reading: The girl tells her lover that because he, a stranger to her still, has parted from her, the flower-filled hair loses its natural grace and her eyes rain without ceasing until the fire-bright gem jewel on her breast is soaked.
232.nuance: ஏதிலாளனை calls him a stranger: in courtship he has no bond she can name, so his leaving is the act of an outsider, and the word itself presses for marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: an unwed lover's parting in courtship, kurinji's union and its occasions

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the first person என் கண்ணே and the second person நீ show the girl speaking to the lover

233.reading: The friend tells the hill lord that he does not come and the north wind is very cruel, so he should not go back to his rocky land where the waterfall rushes down the hard slope sweeping away choice gems.
233.nuance: The waterfall that strips the mountain of its gems as it runs away may suggest the lover who takes the girl's beauty with him when he goes, but the image does no act of a person in the situation, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard mountain and the cold north wind

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; செல்லல் (do not go) is a plea to the lover, and வருவை அல்லை reproaches his absences

234.reading: The friend tells the lover that the girl's bright bangles slip and her fair brow turns pale because she, who sees his chest close beside her in dreams, never sees it awake.
234.nuance: The dream is not a comfort here but the measure of the lack: the closeness she has asleep (துன்னி) makes the waking absence the cause of the pallor.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers of courtship meet only in her dreams

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; she names the girl as இவள் and addresses the lover with நின் மார்பே

comparisons.tenor: the rarity of the lovers' time together

235.reading: The friend says that time for lovers is as hard to come by as a clear sky falling into one's hand, and asks whether, holding him so the chosen jewels jingle, they should say 'we will not part' or rise and go.
235.nuance: Read with the next poem, எழுகமோ (shall we rise) is the first hint of going away with him; the two choices are to keep him here or to leave with him.

thinai_evidence.note: embrace and the refusal to part

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the inclusive plural (என்கமோ, எழுகமோ) is the friend speaking for the girl and herself to the lover

236.reading: The friend tells the lover that the mother has come to know, gossip has risen, and the cruel north wind assails the good house till its tall mansion is desolate, so they will go to his town: shall they set out?
236.nuance: மலையும் is best taken as the verb (it assails) with the wind as subject; read as 'and the mountain', the line would add the hill to the wind among the things that make home unbearable.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend proposes leaving home with the lover, the paalai situation of elopement, against the colophon's kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; she reports the mother's knowledge and the gossip and proposes going to his town (நும்மூர்)

237.reading: The friend asks the lover where his town lies in relation to that high mountain rising tall, should a time come when desire drives them and the heart aches enough to come and see him.
237.nuance: The innocent question about the way to his town is a threat and a plea at once: if he will not come, they may come to him, which the courting girl cannot do without disgrace.

thinai_evidence.note: his town is placed by the high mountain

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the plural யாம் and நும்மூர் are the friend speaking for the girl to the lover

comparisons.vehicle: வயத்தகர் வாராது மாறினும் குரூஉமயிர்ப் புருவை ஆசையின் அல்கும்
comparisons.tenor: the lover who stays away and the girl who waits for him in longing

ullurai.tenor: the lover who stays away and the girl who waits for him

pairs.situation: the lover turns away and does not come
the girl stays on, waiting in longing

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses wild sheep of the kurinji hill in a kurinji poem, without leaving the land (porul 7.27)

238.reading: The friend tells the lord of the cool great mountain of sounding falls, where the coloured-fleeced ewe stays on in longing even when the long-horned ram turns away and does not come, that her girl's beauty revives whenever he comes here.
238.nuance: புருவை (ewe) and தகர் (ram) are rare in the akam lexicon; the ewe that stays put in desire is the girl who keeps faith while he stays away.

thinai_evidence.note: the wild ram and the mountain of falls

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; she addresses the hill lord and speaks of the girl as இவள்

comparisons.tenor: her arms, smooth and rounded as bamboo

iraicchi.act: the elephant in must, lacking its mate, embraces a rough boulder in her place
iraicchi.sense: even the beast of his land cannot do without its mate, yet the man stays away from the girl

239.reading: The friend tells the lover that since he went back to his good land of hills, where a spotted-faced elephant drunk with must, bees feeding on it, embraces a dark rough boulder taking it for his mate, they will not live if he does not come before the girl's shapely bamboo-smooth arms grow thin.
239.nuance: The elephant's embrace of a stone is longing without its object: even the beast of his land cannot bear to be without its mate, and yet the man stays away.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill elephant and the land of hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the plural வாழேம் is the friend speaking for the girl and herself to the lover

240.reading: The friend tells the lover that they are not ignorant but have come to know: his chest, where striped-winged bees swarm, smells of the hair of the fragrant girl who smells of sandal.
240.nuance: The scent on his chest is the secret union made public to the friend; in a marutham poem the same words would accuse a husband of another woman, but in this kurinji decade the fragrant woman is the friend's own girl, and the friend's knowing is the step before pressing for marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: sandal, the hill tree whose scent she wears

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; she tells the lover she has read the secret from the scent on his chest (நின் மார்பே)

links.note: Kural 1213's woman says she lives because she sees in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; in Ainkurunuru 234 the friend tells the lover that the girl sees his chest in dreams and not awake, and that is why she pales.
links.teaches: The same split between dream and waking presence is the woman's own comfort in the Kural and the friend's evidence of harm in the Sangam poem, so the couplet's consolation is shown to be what an onlooker reads as wasting, and the dream becomes a lever for marriage rather than a way to live.

links.note: Both close on எழுகமோ, shall we rise; 235 sets it against holding him and saying 'we will not part', 236 gives the destination, நும்மூர்ச் செல்கம், we will go to your town.
links.teaches: Read alone, 235's 'shall we rise' could mean only leaving the tryst; the next poem fixes it as setting out for his town and names what forced the choice, the mother's knowing and the gossip, so the decade moves from weighing elopement to proposing it.

links.note: In both the friend tells the lover that the girl will go with him: in Akananuru 107 because she cannot bear his repeated departures, in Ainkurunuru 236 because the mother knows, gossip has spread and the house is desolate.
links.teaches: The friend's offer of elopement is made from two opposite pressures, the grief of his going in the Akananuru and exposure at home in the Ainkurunuru, so udanpokku appears in the anthologies as the answer both to separation and to discovery.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 236's friend says the north wind leaves the good house's tall mansion desolate (நன்மனை நெடுநகர் புலம்புகொள) as a reason to leave; Akananuru 35's mother says the girl left the high-walled good house desolate (நன்னகர் புலம்ப) by going.
links.teaches: The same desolation of the great house is the cause of the girl's going in the friend's plea and its effect in the mother's lament, so the two speakers each blame the empty house on the other side and the elopement is seen whole only from both.

links.note: Both are a friend's reproach to the hill lord for his absences in courtship, with a tusker's embrace in the same words (இரும்பிணர் ... தழு): in Akananuru 78 he clasps his trembling pregnant mate in his rough trunk, in Ainkurunuru 239 he clasps a rough boulder, taking it for his mate.
links.teaches: The one image of a tusker's embrace serves the friend two ways, as the care the man owes the girl when the mate is there and as the blind longing of a beast whose mate is gone, so the reproach can shame the lover either by what the beast does for its mate or by what it suffers without her.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 2 the man asks the pollen-seeking bee whether any flower is more fragrant than his woman's hair; in Ainkurunuru 240 the friend says bee swarms crowd his chest because it smells of the fragrant girl's hair.
links.teaches: The scent of her hair that the lover praises in private to the bee is the very thing that betrays the secret union to the friend, so the bees that witness his boast in one poem become the witnesses against him in the other.

source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers and addressees in thurai_akam are inferred from the poems' pronouns and recorded with a note.

235 line 1 கையுற வீழ்ந்த மையில் வானமொடு is obscure; we read it as a comparison, 'as rare as a clear sky dropping into one's hand', with ஒடு marking the likeness; the sense of the poem turns on it, so 235 is marked uncertain.
236 line 3 மலையும் may be the verb (it assails) or the noun (the mountain); we take the verb.
